<reason>Side B systematically dismantled every pillar of Side A's case while maintaining tight internal consistency. Side B proved that paying to avoid an emission in India while continuing to burn coal in Ohio does not result in net-zero emissions, and showed that unlimited cheap offsets crowd out the commercial demand needed to scale down costs in hard-to-abate sectors. Side A dropped the physical equivalence argument in the first rebuttal, made a deeply flawed claim that retail and tech supply chains do not run through the Global South, and fatally contradicted itself between [A2.1], [A4.1], and [A5.2] on whether executives would ever fund domestic retrofits while cheap offsets remain available.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's pressure question [B3.1] and follow-up in [B4.3] and [B5.1], which forced Side A to admit in [A4.1] that no profit-driven executive would pay hundreds of dollars per ton for internal retrofits while cheap offsets are unlimited—directly contradicting Side A's own defense in [A2.1] and [A5.2] that firms would finance both simultaneously.</best_rebuttal>
